# 2010 Lincoln MKS - Wobbling/shaking side to side

When a vehicle exhibits body roll or lateral shifting on a smooth road after a suspension rebuild, it is rarely a simple "settling in" issue. The symptoms you are describingâa car that feels like it is constantly hitting potholes even when driving straightâindicate a geometric mismatch or a component failure within the new assembly. Since the steering wheel remains steady and there are no audible noises, the problem is isolated to the suspension linkage or mounting points affecting chassis rigidity.

The most common culprit in this specific scenario involves the strut mount bushings or the strut tower pads. When replacing shocks on a 2010 Lincoln MKS, technicians must ensure that the old rubber isolators are not compromised or that the new ones are correctly seated. If the strut mounts were left stiff or if the torque specifications were not met during reassembly, the shock absorber cannot articulate properly relative to the engine bay. This creates a rigid connection that transfers every minor irregularity directly into the cabin as a shaking sensation.

Another frequent oversight occurs with the lower control arm bushings. You mentioned these were installed alongside the shocks, but the method of installation is critical. If the polyurethane or rubber bushings were not pressed in evenly, they can bind. A bound bushing prevents the suspension from absorbing road noise and vibration, causing the entire body to shudder laterally. This mimics the feeling of driving over a rough surface. It is essential to verify that the bolts securing these bushings are torqued to the manufacturer's exact specifications. Over-torquing can crush the rubber, while under-torquing allows for play that manifests as body roll.

Alignment is the third variable to investigate immediately. When shocks and bushings are replaced, the vehicle's camber and caster angles often shift. Even if the car was aligned before reassembly, the suspension geometry may have settled differently once the new components were under load. If the alignment was performed with worn-out jacking points or without accounting for the specific kinematics of the MKS platform, the wheels could be tracking incorrectly relative to each other. This misalignment causes the tires to scrub against the road surface, generating the lateral vibration you feel in the floorboard and seat cushions without affecting the steering wheel.

There is also the possibility of a worn sway bar link or bushing that went unnoticed during the rebuild. If one side of the chassis is more flexible than the other due to a failed bushing on the anti-roll bar, the vehicle will twist under acceleration or braking, creating that unsettling side-to-side motion. The fact that this issue persists after running errands suggests a mechanical fault rather than an adjustment period.

Before taking the car back in, inspect the strut tower nuts. Ensure they are tight and that there is no visible movement in the upper shock mount. If the previous repair shop did not clean the mounting surfaces before installing the new hardware, debris could be preventing a solid lock-up. Request a visual inspection of the suspension geometry using an alignment rack to confirm that the new bushings are functioning within their intended range of motion.

If the issue persists after verifying these mechanical connections, it may indicate that the original frame or subframe has developed fatigue cracks around the mounting points, a known weakness in high-mileage Lincolns from this era. In such cases, replacing the bushings alone will not resolve the structural flexing until the underlying frame integrity is addressed.
